adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The state Public Utilities Commission opened its rate case hearing on Tuesday morning with testimony from consumer advocates, utility executives and lawyers from the attorney general's office. The hearing was held in the commission's chambers downtown and was streamed live for residents who could not attend in person. For more than three hours, the five commissioners questioned witnesses about a proposed increase of $340 million, the largest the utility has requested in a decade.

Staff for the commission began by summarizing the docket. They told the panel that the company's own filings showed a widening gap between the rates it collects and the costs it reports, and they recommended that the commission order an independent audit before any increase takes effect. The presiding commissioner asked whether the statute gave the commission authority to impose such an audit, and the commission's general counsel replied that the relevant section of the public utilities code had been amended by the legislature two years ago and clearly permitted it.

A lawyer for the utility disputed that reading. She argued that the legislature had intended the amendment to apply only to municipal utilities, and that the commission would exceed its authority if it treated the provision as a general grant of power. Two commissioners pressed her on the point, noting that the department had issued guidance in the spring that took the opposite view.

The hearing then moved to the question of reliability. An engineer retained by the commission described the condition of substations along the coast and said that several had failed inspection. Under questioning, he conceded that the company had requested deferrals of maintenance spending in each of the past three years, and that the deferrals had been approved by the commission's engineering staff without a formal vote.

A consumer advocate from the ratepayers' association testified that households in the service territory already paid among the highest bills in the region. She presented a table comparing the company's rates with those of neighboring districts and asked the commission to freeze the increase until the audit was complete. The chairman of the senate energy committee, who attended as a member of the public, said afterward that he expected the legislature to revisit the statute if the commission did not act.

The company's chief executive issued a statement after the hearing saying that the request was necessary to fund upgrades and that the utility would cooperate with any review. A spokesman for the governor said the administration would wait for the commission's decision before commenting.

The commission is scheduled to hear closing arguments next month and must issue a written order within ninety days. Any party may then seek review in the state court of appeals, where similar rate decisions have been reversed twice in the past five years. The full record, including exhibits and transcripts, will be posted on the department's website when the proceeding concludes. A final decision is expected before the winter rate season begins.
